audience.programmeDescription: Environmental Sciences at Wageningen combines natural science, social science and technology to investigate pollution, climate change, resource use and environmental solutions. The programme is taught in English and remains rooted in the natural sciences.

provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.name: Econometrics
provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

audience.programmeDescription: Environmental Sciences at Wageningen combines natural science, social science and technology to investigate pollution, climate change, resource use and environmental solutions. The programme is taught in English and remains rooted in the natural sciences.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes explore environmental problems through integrated science and circular solutions, ecosystem resilience, or policy and economic methods. WUR includes a more prescribed chemistry, air-quality, microbiology/toxicology, engineering and environmental-law sequence. Thesis entry for the selected WUR course combination still needs confirmation.

curriculum.routeLabel: Interdisciplinary Environmental Challenges; Mathematics A preparation
curriculum.limitation: WUR lists 180 EC for this example. Thesis entry depends on the chosen chair group’s specialisation preparation; the applicable preparation for this course combination still needs confirmation.

componentNotes.common-math-choice: This example uses Mathematics Applied: Introduction for VWO Mathematics A. Students with Mathematics B take Statistics 1 instead; the choice follows prior preparation and study advice.
componentNotes.common-solutions: General, laboratory and fieldwork safety are non-credit requirements for the relevant practical activities. They are not added to the 180 EC.
componentNotes.spec-nexus: The selected specialisation combines this 6 EC nexus course with 12 EC of social-science and 12 EC of natural-science/technology options. Other permitted combinations may use 6–18 EC in each of those groups, with up to 6 EC of optional quantitative methods, while keeping 30 EC in total.
componentNotes.spec-law: This example selects the first two listed social-science options: International and EU Environmental Law and Environmental Economics. This is one permitted choice, not a claim that both are compulsory for every student in the specialisation.
componentNotes.spec-renewable: This example selects Renewable Energy Technologies and the paired Organic Chemistry 1 and Environmental Organic Chemistry units from the natural-science/technology group. Laboratory safety applies to the chemistry practicals.
componentNotes.common-project: WUR requires a 12 EC international, field-based transdisciplinary project with a commissioner and local stakeholders. It assumes at least 60 EC from the first two years and requires fieldwork safety. Separate UCR projects do not reproduce this coordinated course.
componentNotes.common-micro-tox: WUR teaches microbial cells, growth and metabolism alongside chemical toxicity, risk assessment and a microbiology practical. Introductory life science at UCR is not the same specialist laboratory and toxicology sequence.
componentNotes.common-skills-academy: The Skills Academy connects programme experiences through personal leadership, reflection and a progress portfolio. A general research project is not its direct equivalent.
componentNotes.common-air: WUR studies pollutant emissions, atmospheric transport, chemical conversion, deposition and health effects with models and observations. General climate-change study does not reproduce this air-quality sequence.
componentNotes.spec-env-organic: WUR studies organic pollutants, their reactivity, breakdown and environmental stability after Organic Chemistry 1. UCR’s metal recovery and soil-remediation work does not reproduce this dedicated organic-chemistry sequence.
componentNotes.free-choice: Thirty EC remains available for a minor and/or individually chosen electives. An optional 12 or 18 EC internship would use part of this space; no internship is required in this example.
componentNotes.thesis: The required individual thesis is 12 EC. Entry requires at least 102 BES credits, all 60 first-year credits, and preparation for the chosen chair group. The applicable chair-group preparation for this course combination still needs confirmation.

notes.text: The UCR programmes combine actual environmental science, ecological study, circular-resource and energy analysis with governance or policy/economic methods. WUR has a more prescribed general/organic chemistry, air-quality, microbiology/toxicology, engineering and environmental-law sequence, plus coordinated international field research and an individual thesis. UCR’s optional 15 EC independent research is additional to the illustrated 180 EC.
